Q: Build .NET Framework 4.7.1 ASP.NET apps without Visual Studio A:

Yes its possible. You're only missing the web build targets (Microsoft.WebApplication.targets), which ship with MSBuild from Visual Studio, not the Framework MSBuild you used.

Install Build Tools for Visual Studio — a free standalone download that needs no Visual Studio license, so the Community 250-FTE rule doesn't apply. Pick the web/ASP.NET and .NET Framework components. Then restore packages (msbuild /t:Restore) and build with its MSBuild:

C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\MSBuild\Current\Bin\MSBuild.exe YourSolution.sln

Do check the Build Tools license terms yourself before rolling it out company-wide.

Q: Why are FAT32 disks limited to 4 GB files? A:

FAT32 stores each file's size in a single 32-bit field in the directory entry. A 32-bit number can hold at most 2^32 − 1 bytes, which is 4,294,967,295 bytes, or one byte short of 4 GB. There is no bigger field to write the size into, so the file system simply cannot record a size past that point.

That's the whole reason. It's not about disk space or cluster count. It's that the "how big is this file" slot is only 4 bytes wide, and 4 bytes maxes out at ~4 GB.

You can't overcome it while staying on FAT32; the limit is baked into the on-disk format. To store bigger files you use a file system with a wider size field, like exFAT, NTFS, or ext4.

Q: How do I get the autocomplete hints to work for items in my generic dictionary class? A:

The reason is that your Items class inherits from the bare dict, not from dict[K, I]. When you write class Items[K, I](dict), the type parameters K and I that you declared on Items are never connected to the dictionary's key and value types. To the type checker, the base is just dict[Unknown, Unknown]. So dict.__getitem__ returns an unknown type, which behaves like Any, and you get no completion hints on Any.

That's also why hannah. works but emily['Hannah']. doesn't. hannah came straight from the Person(...) constructor, so the checker knows it's a Person. But emily['Hannah'] goes through __getitem__, and since your base dict has no value type, the checker loses track and hands you back Any. Same object at runtime, but the checker can't prove the type anymore.

The fix is to pass your type parameters into the base class:

from typing import Self
 
class Items[K, I](dict[K, I]):
    def add_item(self, key: K, item: I):
        # some additional logic here not shown
        self[key] = item
 
class Person(Items[str, 'Person']):
    def __init__(self, name: str, parent: Self | None):
        self.name = name
        self.parent = parent
        if parent is not None:
            parent.add_item(self.name, self)

Now Person resolves to dict[str, Person], so __getitem__ is known to return Person. emily['Hannah']. will give you the name and parent hints just like hannah. does.

The one line that matters is (dict) becoming (dict[K, I]). dict is already generic in the type stubs, so once you bind K and I to it, all the indexing type info comes along for free and your autocomplete lights up.

Q: View query results from a PL/SQL block without PUT_LINE, RETURN_RESULTS, or CREATE? A:

The thing to accept first is that a generic BI or reporting client will only show and export what a plain SELECT hands back. An anonymous block has no clean way to "return" a result set to that kind of client, so the fix is usually to stop thinking in PL/SQL loops and push the date-range logic into set-based SQL. That happens to also kill the redundant code you're trying to get rid of.

Let me go through why your attempts do what they do. The inline function that returns SYS_REFCURSOR shows up as (DATASET) because a cursor is a nested thing, not a flat column. Your grid sees one column whose value is "a cursor," so it just shows a placeholder you can drill into. There's no flat rowset there to export. The BULK COLLECT loop gives you "x rows affected" because it runs entirely on the server and never emits a rowset at all; the rows land in a PL/SQL variable that dies when the block ends, so nothing gets sent back. And the ODCIVARCHAR2LIST trick works because that's a real SQL collection type, so SELECT * FROM TABLE(...) can flatten it, but it's a single VARCHAR2 column by design. To get several typed columns you'd need a SQL object type plus a table-of-that-object type, and creating those needs CREATE TYPE, which you said you don't have. So all three roads hit the same wall: without CREATE you can't build a proper multi-column table function, and a client like ODP.NET won't turn a ref cursor or DBMS_OUTPUT into an exportable grid on its own.

One more note so you don't chase it: DBMS_SQL.RETURN_RESULT and implicit results in general are consumed by tools like SQL*Plus, SQLcl, and SQL Developer. They're not a general ODP.NET feature, so they won't help you here. Worth checking against your exact client version, but that's my understanding.

So here's the route I'd take. Your real goal is one query instead of many near-duplicate CTEs grouped by day, month, and year. You don't need PL/SQL for that. Two plain-SQL tools cover it: GROUPING SETS (or ROLLUP) to get several date grains from one pass over the data, and a label column so each output row tells you what it is. Something like this:

SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN GROUPING(d_day)   = 0 THEN 'DAILY'
    WHEN GROUPING(d_month) = 0 THEN 'MONTHLY'
    ELSE 'YEARLY'
  END                                   AS grain,
  COALESCE(d_day, d_month, d_year)      AS period,
  SUM(amount)                           AS total_amount,
  COUNT(*)                              AS row_count
FROM (
  SELECT
    TRUNC(dt)          AS d_day,
    TRUNC(dt, 'MM')    AS d_month,
    TRUNC(dt, 'YYYY')  AS d_year,
    amount
  FROM my_table
)
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ( (d_day), (d_month), (d_year) )
ORDER BY grain, period;

One scan, one rowset, every grain in it, and it exports fine because it's just a SELECT. For the "equivalent queries on similar tables" part, stack them with UNION ALL and add a source label instead of writing separate queries:

SELECT 'TABLE_A' AS source, id, amount, dt FROM table_a
UNION ALL
SELECT 'TABLE_B' AS source, id, amount, dt FROM table_b

Then wrap that in the grouping query above. Now the near-duplicate logic lives in exactly one place and you never left plain SQL.

If the shape of the query really has to be built at runtime, the honest answer is that a generic BI client needs a ref cursor bound as an OUT parameter, and the client has to be the one binding it. ODP.NET can do this in .NET code with an OracleDbType.RefCursor output parameter, but whether your BI layer exposes that is the real question, and you'd have to check that tool's docs. If it can't bind an OUT ref cursor, dynamic PL/SQL won't reach the grid no matter how you write it.

Given the wall you're hitting, my honest recommendation is the set-based rewrite. It removes the redundancy you set out to fix, and a plain SELECT is the one thing every client here will show and export.

A couple of things to confirm on your end before you lean on this: whether your BI tool can bind an OUT SYS_REFCURSOR, since that decides if the dynamic route is even open, and your Oracle version, since WITH FUNCTION and GROUPING SETS both work on 12c and up but not on older releases.

Q: How large does the FAT structure and how large is the file? A:

A. How large does the FAT structure need to be accommodate a 1GB (2^30 bytes) disk?

The FAT file system splits the space into clusters, then has a table (the "cluster allocation table" or FAT) with an entry for each cluster (to say if it's free, faulty or which cluster is the next cluster in a chain of clusters). To work out size of the "cluster allocation table" divide the total size of the volume by the size of a cluster (to determine how many clusters and how many entries in the "cluster allocation table"), then multiply by the size of one entry, then maybe round up to a multiple of the cluster size or not (depending on which answer you want - actual size or space consumed).

B. What is the largest theoretical le size supported by the FAT structure from part (A)?

The largest file size supported is determined by either (whichever is smaller):

  • the size of "file size" field in the file's directory entry (which is 32-bit for FAT32 and would therefore be 4 GiB); or

  • the total size of the space minus the space consumed by the hidden/reserved/system area, cluster allocation table, directories and faulty clusters.

For a 1 GiB volume formatted with FAT32, the max. size of a file would be determined by the latter ("total space - sum of areas not usable by the file").

Note that if you have a 1 GiB disk, this might (e.g.) be split into 4 partitions and a FAT file system might be given a partition with a fraction of 1 GiB of space. Even if there is only one partition for the "whole" disk, typically (assuming "MBR partitions" and not the newer "GPT partitions" which takes more space for partition tables, etc) the partition begins on the second track (the first track is "reserved" for MBR, partition table and maybe "boot manager") or a later track (e.g. to align the start of the partition to a "4 KiB physical sector size" and avoid performance problems caused by "512 logical sector size").

In other words, the size of the disk has very little to do with the size of the volume used for FAT; and when questions only tell you the size of the disk and don't tell you the size of the partition/volume you can't provide accurate answers.

What you could do is state your assumptions clearly in your answer, for example:

"I assume that a "1 GB" disk is 1000000 KiB (1024000000 bytes, and not 1 GiB or 1073741824 bytes, and not 1 GB or 1000000000 bytes); and I assume that 1 MiB (1024 KiB) of disk space is consumed by the partition table and MBR and all remaining space is used for a single FAT partition; and therefore the FAT volume itself is 998976 KiB."

Q: The FAT, Linux, and NTFS file systems A:

FAT32 uses 32-bit numbers to store cluster numbers. It supports larger disks and files up to 4 GiB in size.

As far as I understand the topic, FAT uses File Allocation Tables which are used to store data about status on disk. It appears that it doesn't use trees. I could be wrong though.

Q: Represent more than 20 levels in a glmtree() A:

The cleanest fix is ggparty, which was built partly for this problem. Its geom_edge_label() has two arguments aimed directly at wide factor splits: splitlevels, which lets you choose which levels of the split to plot, and max_length, which truncates the level names to a given length. Rdrr.io

So you can either truncate:

r

library(ggparty)
ggparty(tree) +
  geom_edge() +
  geom_edge_label(max_length = 3) +
  geom_node_splitvar() +
  geom_node_plot(gglist = list(...))

or split the level list into chunks and stack them so they don't run off the edge:

r

ggparty(tree) +
  geom_edge() +
  geom_edge_label(splitlevels = 1:8,   nudge_y =  0.03) +
  geom_edge_label(splitlevels = 9:16,  nudge_y =  0.00) +
  geom_edge_label(splitlevels = 17:29, nudge_y = -0.03) +
  geom_node_splitvar()

The "On the edge" vignette has a worked example of exactly this on a ctree with a many-level factor. shift is also useful there, it slides the label along the edge if things collide.

If you want to stay in base partykit, edge_simple() takes abbreviate (logical or integer) and justmin, so plot(tree, edge_panel = edge_simple(tree, abbreviate = 3, justmin = 15)) gets you some of the way, though it's much less controllable than the ggparty route.

Two other things worth knowing regardless of which you pick. plot(tree[5]) plots the subtree rooted at node 5, which is often more readable than fighting to fit the whole thing on one page. And partykit:::.list.rules.party(tree) gives you the split conditions for every terminal node as plain strings, so you can draw the tree with short or no edge labels and print the full rules as a caption underneath.

One more option that isn't dummification: just rename the factor levels to short codes before fitting and keep a lookup table for the legend. levels(d$i_mode) <- sprintf("M%02d", seq_along(levels(d$i_mode))). The model is mathematically identical since you're only relabelling, and 29 two-character codes fit on an edge where 29 real names never will.

Q: What is the maximum file size and filesystem size in a 32-bit system? A:

File systems (ext3, ext4, XFS, etc.) all have theoretical and supported limits. Theoretical limits (16 TB on ext3) are based on the on-disk data structures of the underlying file system, supported is what has been tested (4 TB).

The supported limit can vary in most file systems and is tunable by the administrator depending on whether you want to have large number of large files (ISO images, images, etc. - means less metadata on-disk) or small files (GIF images - larger percent of disk is required to store file system metadata). Again the file size and file system limits are always different values.

Q: Apache Zookeeper: Unable to access data directory A:

In the configuration file, this line

dataDir=/var/zookeeper/

appears twice. Removing that line solves the issue.
